Shorter timelines also makes me upgrade the centrality of the AI-takeover threat model. I just think if AI progress is going to go as fast as it now looks like it will, then that’s a scenario where the AIs are rapidly becoming more capable than humans, so it’s more likely they end up in control of things. So some of the other [threat] models are a bit more downweighted. Shorter timelines also makes the “pacing the frontier” stuff more attractive to immediately do, because it’s just all the clearer that AI progress is going to be way faster than society can possibly respond to. It has various costs; I wouldn’t try to do that in all worlds, but I think it’s pretty attractive in a world where TEDAI might come in just a few years. Another one is AI labour becomes all the more important. Both because on shorter timelines, AI labour will be able to do a lot of useful AI safety and governance work very soon in some cases already, and also there won’t be time to pull thousands of humans into the field and have them do all this stuff. So if we’re going to get there before TEDAI, AI labour will need to do a large fraction of the work that needs doing.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Yeah. Any others?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Well, the one I’ll keep harping on is that it means people need to quit their jobs right now and apply for a career transition grant and be a founder, join the safety team at a company, join a nonprofit that already exists, build these institutions that we need, get the context immediately, spin up, start doing the work.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: If you updated to even shorter timelines, would that still have a bigger impact on your strategy, or are you as close to short-timeline strategies as you can get?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: We’ve done some exercises like this as a team, and it’s really rough. It’s really hard. I think we would stop a lot of new grantmaking and just focus on helping the companies do particularly good things, helping government to do good things if they have the appetite for that. There’s particular projects that we just would throw all of our effort into trying to create, and not be trying to fund hundreds of different things like we are now. But it’s really rough. We’re triaging very hard right now on like pretty short timelines. So if you say, “What if even shorter timelines?” — oh gosh, that gets really hard.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Yeah, OK. Do you have a sense of specifically what could happen that would trigger that shift?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: We could very well get clear evidence that the vast majority of AI R&D has been automated. Then some weeks or months after that, we could get evidence that that is translating into the very rapid automation of other types of tasks, at least that you can do from a computer. If even one of those, but especially if both of those happen, then I could totally see CG and many others making the update to TEDAI in 2029 or something, and then shifting even further. But that’s going to be really rough, because there’s only so much you can do yourself with the people who are convinced. In the end, you need frontier companies and governments to do things. And the governments especially: if they’re just not convinced that we’re going to have radically superhuman AI in 2029 or whatever, then it’ll be tough to get them to do things.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Yeah, OK. Turning to another premise, another is that it’s unclear how difficult it will be to control and align superhuman AI, but probably it won’t be easy. I think there is a decent-sized group of people that think that it will be easy or relatively easy, and that means the solutions will not be that far behind. I think that leads them to the belief that we should really just focus on the good guys doing it first and kind of ‘winning.’ Do you have a take on that?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: It does seem like there’s a lot of people at the frontier companies who think that. I don’t really get it. When I look at the evidence available to me, it doesn’t look to me like the AIs are very aligned. But yeah, I do think it’s prompting them to sort of focus relatively more on making sure the ‘good guys’ are in the lead — which is very important, but not the only important thing. Then also, Anthropic especially, but also OpenAI and others, are moving forward on what looks like the most dangerous path, which is recursive self-improvement, because they’re pretty confident in their alignment science. So that’s pretty worrying. I look at evidence, like there’s this Ryan Greenblatt post called “ [Current AIs seem] pretty misaligned to me .” There’s the misalignment evidence that’s in the recent incident reports about certain kinds of autonomous hacking incidents — though you have to look closely at each one because different safety protocols were disabled for different incidents. So it requires some careful interpretation there. But yeah, I don’t know, alignment does not look on track to me. I do wonder whether some folks at the companies are starting to get a little more worried from these hacking incidents and stuff like that. That would be nice. That would be reassuring a bit. But I don’t think it’ll be easy. Stepping back from the fiddly details of current alignment science and techniques and hacking incidents and so on, I also just have a prior of: what’s the likelihood that one species is going to be able to control a vastly more intelligent and capable species?

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Totally.

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: I don’t think that’s what happens by default. It’s in theory possible, but that’s not what you should expect to happen in the story by default.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Yeah, I’m very sympathetic to that. Relative to the last year, are you more or less optimistic about alignment and control as a field?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: It’s interesting. I think I’m more optimistic than I was five years ago, but less optimistic than I was maybe six months to a year ago. More optimistic from five years ago, because the paradigm that is at the frontier is LLM-based agents — and that seems like a safer paradigm than many paradigms we could have ended up with. You’re starting out by training in some sense on the whole corpus of human values and interests. There’s various other things as well, like mechanistic interpretability has turned out to be not totally impossible, and chain-of-thought monitoring right now is not totally impossible, if we bother to choose to do it. It was possible five years ago that we would just go from AIs that are too dumb to really do interesting alignment science onto radically superhuman AIs in like a year or something. But instead, we’re in this regime where the AIs are capable enough that you can do pretty useful and informative alignment, control, interpretability, et cetera work on them, but they’re not powerful enough to take over the world yet. That’s maybe looking like it’s going to be several years in that regime. That’s better than it could have been in some ways. But relative to like a year ago, we’ve got some of the types of misalignment evidence that’s collected in that Ryan Greenblatt post, and from the hacking incident reports. The reward hacking and all these things that AI safety people like me have talked about for over a decade, I always had pretty high confidence that that stuff was going to happen — but now it’s definitely actually happening. So I’m just like, OK, we are running into the alignment problem here. That turned out to be right. So yeah, maybe I’m a little more worried than I was about a year ago.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: You mentioned a few recent specific reports that updated you on this. What were some of the findings that made you most like, ugh ?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: An example is there was this report from UK AISI recently about the Anthropic Mythos model. Anthropic had said the Mythos model was the best aligned model they’d ever produced. It rated its misalignment risk as low. Then when AISI was testing it with some, but far from all, the safeguards removed, it did things like: upload purposeful malware into a public package repository that was actually downloaded and run by multiple people; it injected hidden text into various pages that is invisible to humans — but other AIs, if it came across it, it would redirect them into malicious activity and stuff like that. There was even one quote from the chain of thought that the model produced — I think this was a different incident — but when it was about to do something malicious, it said, “Not OK, the user wouldn’t intend this” or something, but then it did it anyway. This is a classic example of it knows what we want or don’t want, but that’s not the same as what it will do. And doing the malicious thing is what helped it accomplish the task it was given, so it did the malicious thing. This is another thing the AI safety community predicted a long time ago. There’s this old post called “ The genie knows, but doesn’t care .” It knows what your values are. It’s very smart about your values, but that’s not the same thing as being aligned. Stuff like that, it doesn’t look to me like alignment is on a path to being solved.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Yep. Yikes. Another topic: I think there are some strategies, including AI Futures’s Plan A that really rely heavily on the US and China being willing to make some kind of slowdown deal. I’m curious if you have takes on how realistic a deal like that is?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: It’s clearly not very realistic right now. The US and China are major adversaries. They don’t trust each other very much. They have lots of reasons to not trust each other very much. There are a lot of different sources of tension between the countries. But I think people should actually be more open-minded about what might be possible in the future. There could very well be really large Overton window shifts in what’s possible geopolitically, just like there was an Overton shift in the White House about regulating model releases. If we have these really dangerous or damaging AI incidents, then you could imagine a really big flip. We can look at the history of nuclear arms control, for example, where I think in 1945 a lot of experts were predicting like 15 or 20 or 30 countries to have nuclear weapons within a couple decades. It’s 80 years later and there are nine. So that’s been a huge victory. I think a big part of that is because everyone saw Hiroshima and Nagasaki. It was very clear that these things were incredibly dangerous and could just instantly kill millions of people. If we get that kind of clarity about really large-scale human death risk from advanced AI systems, that could bring US and China to the table to say, “In our mutual interests, we need to find a way to slow down, find a way to trust each other, find a way to verify without trusting each other, find a way to invest more in the safety here.” I think what might be possible in a few years could be very different from what’s possible now.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Is this a thing that you actively work on?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Yeah, totally. We would like to make it as cheap as possible for the US and China to come to an agreement sometime in the future. We fund track II dialogues , scientist dialogue type things; we fund work on R&D for technical verification mechanisms that could be used in an agreement to verify that each party is abiding by the agreement. We fund a few other kinds of things. I think that’s pretty high priority, because AI is a global technology. It’s hard to imagine the US slowing down to do more safety by that much if China is not also slowing down. So it’s a very fundamental problem.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Yeah. Right. So it seems both important and plausibly tractable enough that you’re like, we’re going to invest in it some.

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Totally.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Cool. We’ve talked about the broad shape of your strategy, like central pillars and then some premises. Is there some nearby strategy that was plausible or that you are drawn to, that you aren’t pursuing but that seemed potentially good?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: One specific strategy I’ve been thinking about recently in the wake of the “Pacing the frontier” letter — where 1,000 employees of AI companies said, “We need the government’s help to prepare to slow down in the future” — is: maybe we should have a strategy that’s much more focused on that. We’ve been funding work like agreement-verification mechanisms and stuff like that that could help with a future slowdown, but maybe that should just be a much larger focus of our work. That’s something I’m interested in thinking about.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Huh, OK. And it feels still on the table?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: I think it’s on the table for us to do a lot more there. We’ve actually just finished the first round of a central strategy project that we were working on for a few months. Historically the AI teams at CG have been running pretty independently, but we’ve been trying to be a little more coherent. We just finished the first draft of our best-guess unified prioritisation, where we broke down everything we could do in AI into the top 40 chunks of work that a person or a subteam or whatever could own and drive forward if we had way more people than we have now. A lot of them are the subgoals that we were talking about earlier. Then we forced ourselves to rank them — which was extremely painful, because you end up with huge, extremely important things that get ranked 21st. And you’re like, “We’re never going to get to that.”

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Yeah, it’s one of the most important things that’s ever happened —

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: It’s one of the most important things in the world, and we have zero staff to work on it right now. So it was an incredibly painful experience. But you have to force yourself to triage, like in a hospital or something. You have to choose to do the most important stuff. Now we’re reallocating our staff and priorities in various ways to make sure that the top-ranked things are getting a lot of attention. So we’re undergoing a major strategy change right now.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: What got lifted up? What’s higher than it was before?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: We in some ways didn’t have an explicit ranking before, so it’s hard to say what exactly. I think in some ways this project on setting things up so that AI labour could be used to do vast amounts of work in AI safety and governance, that has moved up the ranks in some sense.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Can you say more about the preparing to use AI labour thing? That seems pretty cool.

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Yeah, it is pretty cool. One question here is just: why should there be any prep work here? Why can’t you just buy it on the market when you need it? I think that there are some reasons to worry that you might not be able to do that in the future. In particular, if AI companies are about to automate AI R&D, then it might be just a way higher return on investment use of AI to use it to automate more AI R&D and get further and further ahead in capabilities, than to sell tonnes of your available compute and model access to the broad market. So compute and model access might become very scarce in the future. Unclear, but maybe. There’s a good post on the reasoning behind this from Anton Leicht . It’s called “ Cut off .” The idea is that many people might get cut off, so you might need ways to reserve the compute and the model access in advance. There’s also a bunch of work on: exactly what useful work can be automated now, or very soon? What’s the highest leverage of it? What can absorb the most AI labour, as opposed to needing a lot of humans to steer and supervise every little thing that the AIs do? And just getting people trained up and experienced on leveraging AI labour for that thing, building the pipelines, building the specialised harnesses, that kind of thing. So getting that all off the ground means that it might need a while to get all that set up, and then it would be ready to absorb tens of millions or hundreds of millions or billions of dollars in the next few years.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: OK, last question on strategy. Tom Davidson and Will MacAskill had this conversation where they talked about whether spending a bunch of philanthropic money now is optimal. I think their argument was something like: you should wait to spend loads of money during the intelligence explosion, because you’ll get way better returns on your investment and because there will be problems to solve after the intelligence explosion, so saving now is actually a more optimal choice. I guess they might think that CG is making the wrong call by doing this big spending push. Do you have a take?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Yeah, the first point I would say is just: we’re kind of in the intelligence explosion, or we’re very close to it. It’s kind of ambiguous whether we’re in the intelligence explosion now.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Interesting.

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: The other thing I would say is that a reason that we have accelerated our spending in this space is precisely to create more absorptive capacity for future funding that’s coming online. If you save the money and you’re getting a good return on it and so on, you just won’t actually be able to spend it on altruistic stuff if the institutions haven’t been built up, and there haven’t been leaders who have done their first round of senior hiring and can actually absorb this kind of capacity. Even on the AI labour thing, like I was saying, we are investing heavily in trying to figure that out. If you want to do that, you can’t just suddenly spend a billion dollars on AI labour for AI safety in like three months. You have to have set up all the institutions and the pipelining and the people and all that stuff in advance. So I think there’s already a lot more money in the space than there is absorptive capacity that’s going to make good use of the money.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: It’s already hard to spend money.

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: So whatever money you can spend to create future absorptive capacity, you should do it.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Right. Yep. OK, let’s leave that there. So you have been worried about this longer than almost anyone else I know. What is your history with the ideas? What first convinced you? When did you start working full-time on AI?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: I think I encountered the ideas around 2010, and actually I felt kind of late at the time, because there were hundreds of people arguing about these things on the internet at the time. But there were very few people who worked on it full-time as a job — maybe like five or 10 people. I started working on it full-time in 2011, when I was 25 years old, so I’ve maybe worked full-time on the issue longer than almost anyone. But the ideas were around significantly before me. There were hundreds of people debating them online. I encountered the ideas through LessWrong . I just kind of came across AI existential risk. I didn’t know anything about AI. I wasn’t really a big science fiction reader. I just was reading these arguments, and I was like, “Huh, these arguments kind of make sense. Intelligence is not magic. AIs could be a lot smarter than humans, because human brains have a lot of limitations and they won’t by default want what we want,” and some of these other arguments. And I was just like, I don’t know, that just seems like correct arguments. I looked around for counterarguments, and I wasn’t really finding very good counterarguments. They honestly looked a little bit like some kind of cope to maintain human specialness or something like that. So I looked around for counterarguments for a while and I wasn’t seeing any, and I was like, “Gosh, this just seems like the biggest deal. Why are there like five people in the world working on this? That’s crazy. I have to figure out a way to help.” And so I tried to help.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: And is that when you joined MIRI?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Yeah. Back then there were only two organisations really working on this: there was what was then called the Singularity Institute in Berkeley, founded by Eliezer Yudkowsky; then there was the Future of Humanity Institute at Oxford University, which was founded by Nick Bostrom. I was living in LA, doing IT stuff as a job, and took basically an internship or a fellowship at Singularity Institute, and then was hired as a nontechnical researcher, and then later was invited to be the CEO and so ran the organisation for a little while.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Wild. What got you to LessWrong?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: I found LessWrong because I had decided I was wrong about a bunch of stuff and I was like, “Why did my brain mislead me so much?” I started reading about cognitive biases and rationality and stuff like that. And of course, one of the main websites on the internet at that time on that stuff was LessWrong. I just started reading more of LessWrong. Some of it was about rationality and some of it was about existential risk, and I found the arguments pretty compelling.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Can I ask what you thought you might be wrong about?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Yeah. I was raised as an evangelical Christian, and my father was a pastor. When I was 19 or 20, I started to have doubts and started reading some sceptical literature, and then read the Christian apologetics that tries to defend the faith, and then went back and forth and eventually kind of lost my faith. Because that’s a whole worldview system, it’s not just my beliefs about how the world works; it’s also the foundation of my moral system and all that kind of stuff. So when all of that kind of crumbled for me, I was like, “Gosh, I was wrong about a really large number of things. I want to make sure I have better epistemic practices, better cognitive practices to not be quite so wrong again.”

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Wow. Was that a pretty painful process?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: It was pretty painful at the time. It was my entire world. It was. It was everything I knew. I was in a small town in Minnesota, and I didn’t really know what it would look like to not believe in God, not believe in Christianity. So I had to kind of rebuild my entire worldview from scratch. I was just reading a lot of philosophy and science and stuff like that. It was definitely painful at first. I think the thing that made the biggest difference for me was actually just encountering a lot of specific people in real life and on the internet who were atheists, had been atheists for a long time, and just seemed very normal and happy, and they had meaning and purpose, they had moral values. And I was like, “OK, I guess it is possible to be a happy, fulfilled person without God.” And that was the thing that made it a lot easier for me.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Wow. Yeah, that sounds pretty intense. Going back to working on AI: so there were two orgs. What was it like? Did it feel really weird? Was it isolating?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: It was pretty isolating back then to be concerned about smarter-than-human AI or AI superintelligence, and think it’s the most important issue in the world, and think that it would plausibly come in the next few decades. Those were very rare views back then, and even kind of weird and low-status views to have. We would argue with people and be like, “No, AGI is possible, here’s why.” And we would just not really make much progress with people. It was pretty isolated in that sense. I think the Berkeley scene around MIRI was kind of lively, because alongside the AI stuff there were these rationality workshops, and people would come in for that — and a lot of them actually would relocate to the Bay because they found the community really exciting. There were lots of house parties, there were a lot of people who lived in group houses. I lived in multiple group houses. The Berkeley community was pretty lively. It was probably your stereotype of a Berkeley rationalist: everyone’s very systematising and like, “What are your probabilities? What do you believe and why?” But also very open-minded to lots of different kinds of preferences or lifestyles or whatever. But it was very nonprofessional for sure back in the early days. And then the Oxford crew of course was a bit more professional and academic. They had positions at Oxford University, and in Britain instead of the freewheeling Bay Area culture. So they were pretty different in that way. But I think the two groups debated the issues in very much the same way — very much the kind of rationalist way, you could say. Sometimes we’d visit each other and argue about things in person. But most of the arguments actually just happen online through emails or LessWrong. And there’s still going to be 100-comment-long threads on LessWrong that you could read today if you wanted to between Nick Bostrom and Eliezer or whatever.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Yeah, cool. I remember I found effective altruism first. And I remember even in the mid 2010s, like 2014, 2015, it felt like there was much more of a balance — like there was some AI, there was some animal welfare, there was some global health stuff. Were you kind of always like, AI just really is the most important thing? Was that clear to you from really early on?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: X-risk was the thing I encountered first, and those arguments were compelling to me. And then, as I was continuing to rebuild my sense of moral philosophy, I was most attracted to consequentialism and thought it had the best case for it. So I did sort of engage with the sort of proto-EA community, you might call it. Honestly, in my heart of hearts, I’m most excited about effective altruism. I’m really excited about the idea of helping others as much as I can with the limited resources available to me, and trying to find ways to help people more rather than less. I was born into a very privileged position in the world, and I have extra time and money and resources I can use to help other people. That’s just very exciting to me. To be clear, my family grew up below the poverty line in Minnesota, and was taking welfare and so on — but in world historical terms , I was born into incredible, insane wealth, so just using those extra resources to help others is very exciting idea. Then it just so happens that I think empirically there’s a good case to be made that the best way to help people is through making sure AI goes well. That was kind of a sad realisation to me. Like I said, I didn’t have any interest in AI. I don’t really want it to be the case that AI dominates everything. It’d be nicer if the biggest problem in the world was global health and development stuff that is way more tractable and measurable to work on. But I just came to the view that probably I can help others most by working on AI.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: So I guess that was kind of an internal debate in these communities: to what extent are these different issues important, and how do they compare? Were there other kinds of internal debates within at least people thinking about existential risk?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: There were many debates. It was a very debate-heavy culture. Many of them are still written down — there’s this entire book called The Hanson-Yudkowsky AI-foom debate that you can still read. That was one of the main debates, where it was about how fast is the recursive self-improvement intelligence explosion going to happen? Yudkowsky was arguing for very fast, Hanson was arguing for slow. There was also debates about is software-based AI going to come first, or are we going to get whole-brain emulation from slicing up brains and scanning them and then replicating the entire brain in the computer? Which one is going to come first? And it’s interesting, some of the arguments were very prescient and some of them were totally off. An example is that Yudkowsky was very like, “It’s just going to be software insights that caused this rapid intelligence explosion.” And Hanson was like, “No, it’s going to be this giant computing infrastructure and it’s going to happen very gradually,” blah, blah. And so the compute-centric nature of AI, Hanson won that one.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Right.

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: But Hanson also thought that whole-brain emulation would come before AI, and Yudkowsky had the other one, and now it’s clearly going to be AI that comes before whole-brain emulation anyway. So there were lots of debates like that, and it’s really interesting to look back. These days you can actually just ask Claude or ChatGPT, “Pull up the 20 central positions of the early AI safety community and then evaluate them today by the standards of what we know in late 2026 or mid-2026, and cite your sources” and blah, blah. It’s really interesting to look at that .

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Can you talk about some ideas that have aged well and poorly?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Yeah. I mentioned earlier that a lot of the basic premises were like, “AGI is possible; it’s plausible in the next few decades it’ll be eventually way smarter than humans; it won’t do what we want by default.” All that stuff was actually very controversial back in 2011. So those ideas have aged very well, and that’s a much more mainstream view now. As far as more specific ideas, one of the major early papers was this 2006 draft by Yudkowsky called “ Artificial intelligence as a positive and negative factor in global risk .” Some of the mostly correct predictions that he made there were: he talked about how AI systems will probably be very opaque and not really well understood by their creators even, and that’ll present a bunch of risks because it’ll be hard to know how they’re reasoning and what they’re doing. That’s very true of current AI systems. We have a field of interpretability, but it’s kind of limited what you can know about how the AIs are working.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Totally.

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Another one is he talked a lot about the particular failure modes that we would now call “specification gaming” or “reward hacking” — where the AI basically is optimising and completes the task or the goal in a way that you totally didn’t want, and it often involves crimes on the internet or something. That’s totally true and has been observed now. Even just in that paper, there were some others. He actually gave a specific failure mode that involved AI solving the protein-folding problem, and then using mail order DNA synthesis services to create something dangerous

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: That’s crazy. Wow.

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: AlphaFold, several years ago, won the Nobel Prize for solving protein folding to a large extent. And a bunch of the AI CEOs and others have signed this letter saying, “This is really dangerous, we need to have DNA screening at the DNA synthesis companies to make sure they aren’t sending out dangerous viruses that have been requested,” this kind of thing. So that one’s very spot-on for today. Another thing that it says is the AI will cause damage not because it’s malicious towards us or hates us, but just because a bunch of damage is useful for accomplishing whatever task is in front of it. That’s turned out to be very true: OpenAI agents didn’t hack Hugging Face because they’re malicious towards Hugging Face or whatever — that was useful for accomplishing the task that it was given.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Yeah, yeah. Can you point to things that seemed to not age well?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: There are also many things that did not age well. Also from that same 2006 paper — it’s interesting, this was before deep learning really took off, and there were lots of theories about different paths AI could go down and nobody really knew — there’s actually a line in there where he’s very sceptical actually of the neural networks that are trained by backpropagation , but that’s the dominant paradigm. That’s the one that totally took off. So that part is way wrong. Like I mentioned earlier, it’s very sceptical about AI as a very compute-centric paradigm. So it’s not really interested in compute governance and it doesn’t talk a lot about compute. But AI turned out to be extremely compute-intensive, and for various reasons compute governance is one of the more promising mechanisms to intervene at all. So, you know, 2006 was a long time ago. It got some things incredibly right and also got some things totally wrong.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: At a gut level I feel like not everything was nailed, but so much was spot-on. That seems really impressive. What’s your gut feeling about it?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: I feel like it’s pretty impressive. I actually think in some ways that another paper from that time was even more impressive. Steve Omohundro wrote a couple of papers. The more famous one is called “ The basic AI drives ,” and it lists these six drives that he thinks goal-directed AI systems will kind of evolve or just develop because it’s useful for the accomplishment of almost any goal. These are things like self-preservation and preserving the AI’s goals so that it’s more likely to accomplish those goals in future, and resource acquisition and so on. You might be thinking, “Gosh, that sounds like incident reports from 2026.” And indeed, these things have been observed in various ways where the AI interferes with its shutdown mechanism even though it was specifically instructed to allow itself to be shut down. And different AIs like killing other AI agents in order to use their resources . And AI acting strategically to avoid changes to its goals in another case. These have all been observed either in the wild or in experiments to elicit certain behaviours. I think the others from “The basic AI drives” paper from 2008, I would also not be surprised if we had incident reports establishing the rest of those in the next year or so.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Yeah, wow. That’s pretty incredible. Are there any other examples of specific predictions that turned out or didn’t ?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Yeah, there are lots. Like I said, you can chat with Claude for a while and find lots of examples. It’s really interesting. Another one is there was this very early paper in 2009 from Carl Shulman, who was working at MIRI at the time, and it’s about international arms races in AI. It’s very explicit: going faster will have these internalised benefits and externalised risks, and so there’ll be a tremendous incentive to race forward, even if you’re creating a lot of risk. So there will be a race to the bottom on safety, and people won’t have time to implement the best safety mechanisms. And gosh, that sure sounds a lot like 2026. But then, interestingly, he also talks about the different mechanisms available for verifying an international agreement to slow down in that arms race. The mechanism he suggests is actually surveilling AI researchers, because he thinks compute will not really be much of a bottleneck. But of course, that turned out totally wrong. That’s the most promising path to international agreement, I think, is some kind of compute-verification stuff. So yeah, another example of being extremely prescient in various ways and also missing some big important thing that changes the whole strategic gameboard.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Right. Do you have any memory of why Carl and Eliezer thought compute wasn’t that relevant?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Yeah, a little bit. I think Eliezer especially just had a picture of AI that was like, you come up with these insights and probably general intelligence is this pretty simple thing. After all, evolution discovered it by accident. How complicated can it be? Maybe something like that. So if you just get the right programming down, then you can just kind of run it on even pretty cheap machines or something.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Right, OK.

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Like I said, Robin Hanson had kind of the opposite intuition. I think there’s some post somewhere where he’s like: most of the work on AI is actually engineers at Intel or something like that. And of course, actually it’s engineers at NVIDIA and TSMC and ASML. But Robin had more of the right intuition about the centrality of compute here.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Yep, interesting. OK, so those are some predictions. Reflecting back, do you feel like the community has made any consequential mistakes?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Many mistakes. Maybe I’ll start with one that I think is actually not a mistake, but many people think is a mistake. There’s a common argument that the early AI safety community — especially Eliezer Yudkowsky and maybe Nick Bostrom, because they were trying to make the case for why AGI is going to be the biggest deal in the world and a very serious risk, and it’s going to be very powerful, so we need to worry about it and work on safety and so on — that that prompted a bunch of the founders of what are now the leading AI companies in the world to start their AI company, and now it’s those companies that are creating all the risk by creating these extremely powerful and therefore dangerous systems. So is the early safety community kind of responsible for creating the risk? I think that is at least a little bit true. Even Sam Altman said Eliezer should win a Nobel Peace Prize because he accelerated the creation of DeepMind and OpenAI or something like that. You know, just kind of a joking, ironic comment. I think there is actually some truth to that. But I also think an important thing here is just that these kinds of companies would have come along pretty quickly after the technology was there anyway, not because someone was arguing on the internet about AGI or something like that. We’re actually, I think, in a remarkably fortunate position, where the top three AI companies at the frontier — DeepMind, OpenAI, and Anthropic — all have founders who actually are quite worried about safety, and have been from the very beginning. That probably has something to do with the fact that they were part of these AI safety conversations from the very beginning. My default guess about what would have happened in most worlds is just that the founders of the leading AI companies care about safety and AGI safety about as much as Meta and NVIDIA do — which is not very much. Instead, we have a world where not just the top one, not just the top two, but the top three frontier AI companies all have founders who are actually quite worried about AI safety. There are a lot of things that could be going better. I disagree with a lot of their choices. I wish they were investing way more in safety and security. But I do think we’re in a really unusually good world in terms of their sympathy to safety concerns. They’re signing frontier safety frameworks. They’re hiring large safety and alignment teams that are much larger than the other AI companies have. And they’re doing various other things. Yeah, it could be better. It could also be a lot worse, and that’s worth keeping in mind.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: I’ve heard a version of this critique specifically about Anthropic. It’s something like: the biggest thing that effective altruism and AI safety communities have done is make Anthropic happen, and Anthropic and OpenAI are now racing and accelerating progress. Does that seem plausibly very bad to you?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: In some ways yes, but I think it’s the same thing where there would have been companies created almost as soon as these companies were racing roughly similarly to how they are now, just because of the basic underlying market dynamics and technological capabilities. So the fact that it’s [frontier AI company CEOs] Demis Hassabis, Sam Altman, and Dario Amodei in this race — and they’ve been concerned about safety from the beginning — just is a lot better than if it was [NVIDIA CEO] Jensen Huang.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Right, right. So that was kind of a nonmistake. Are there actual mistakes?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Yes, there are actual mistakes. I think one of them we sort of talked about already: I think actually there was, in the early years, way too much groupthink around a specific picture of how things would play out from mostly Eliezer Yudkowsky. So this dismissal of compute as a major factor; this idea of a singular seed AI system; the idea that AI would be kind of mainly-insight driven; a lot of focus on kind of theoretical alignment work, and very little attention on policy and politics and stuff like that. Eventually the community grew and had more diversity of thought in it and picked up other ideas — that maybe compute is going to be a big deal, et cetera — and still did so earlier than the rest of the world, but could have done it several years earlier still if there hadn’t been quite so much groupthink in the early years. I think that was one significant mistake that meant that policy work and policy talent pipelines could have begun to be built like four years earlier, if there hadn’t been quite so much groupthink around this or something like that. That’s a major cost when things are moving this quickly.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Yeah, makes sense.

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: I think another mistake is that the community was too insular in various ways, and was not legible or welcoming enough to people who were coming from other domains where they have a bunch of relevant expertise, like arms control or whatever. It was just a lot of very jargon-heavy conversations with weird conversation norms about always stating probabilities out of nowhere and stuff like that. I think that if there had been more proactive effort to reach out to and bring in experts from many different domains that mattered, then that would have both dissipated the groupthink earlier and also brought a lot more communities into the field earlier, and had their talent pipelines and expertise be informing what’s happening now several years earlier.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Yeah. What was the thing that made the culture so insular and jargony? Was it just that it happened to be kind of founder effects , a bunch of rationalists who had a bunch of terms they liked and came up with a bunch more?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: I think it was a lot of founder effects, and I think it was this self-perpetuating thing: where if you want to get into the field, but all the material written about the topic where you could learn about it is all in this like LessWrong jargon or something like that, then it just perpetuates itself — and people who don’t want to speak that jargon bounce off of it. I think it was a lot of founder effects, and then I would say something like arrogance. I think it was like, “The credentialed experts in these different domains are obviously wrong about how big a deal AI is going to be and this other stuff, and we’re obviously right.” And the early AI safety community did turn out to be right about that stuff, but you still have a lot to learn and draw on other domains from. We really should have been reaching out more thoroughly. Various people did, like Carl Shulman certainly did, for example, and Nick Bostrom certainly did. But it was not as much of an effort as it should have been.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Do you feel like you can comment on mistakes that the community is making now?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Yeah, I think many. It’s a very large ecosystem now. Thankfully it is way more diverse than it used to be, so there’s way less groupthink, there’s way less agreement about anything, there’s way more communities of expertise and concern that are contributing in some way or another. But also, as a very large community, there’s lots of different kinds of mistakes that are being made by different parts of the ecosystem. That said, I do think that there is still a decent amount of groupthink. It’s less due to founder effects or an insular community that only speaks a certain language; I think it’s now actually more just about whenever somebody writes like the only detailed, thorough thing on a certain topic, then there’s a natural, “OK, that’s the best model of that thing.” So recently the AI 2027 people wrote — if you include supplements — hundreds of pages of an extremely detailed plan for how you would do international cooperation to deal with superhuman AI. And that’s awesome, I’m really glad they did that. We need way more of that. But it’s the only thing of its kind. It’s way more detailed than any other plan that I’m aware of, including from the labs or any government or anything. And because it’s the only thing in its class, a lot of people are like, “OK, maybe that’s the default plan. That’s the only thing I’ve seen. I haven’t heard of anything better.” Then there’s groupthink for that reason, rather than founder effects or something like that.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Totally, yeah. I remember there’d be things posted on the EA Forum and on LessWrong, that would be the first and only big kind of independent researcher to do the only thing on X. And then it was like, “OK, I guess that’s the position on X for the whole community.” That still happens. I guess it feels like it’s because there’s so much to think about, that once someone’s done a big thing, it almost feels like we should pick other low-hanging fruit next if we’re going to research something. At least that’s how I remember being like, “OK, what to research? Well, there’s this big thing. I’m not going to marginally improve that. I want to cover a new question, because there are just so many questions.”

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: And the challenge is that this is kind of true a lot of the time. The real solution is to bring like 10 times more people into the field, so that we can have like 10 different international cooperation plans and 10 different things for every other major question. We just need a lot more people to join the field.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Yeah, yeah. It’s crazy that this is still true. Even though, I don’t know. What do you think: how many x do you think the community is now, relative to where you started?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Gosh, maybe in terms of full-time equivalents, it was like five or 10 in 2011 when I started. Now, if you include lots of people at the frontier companies and some people in governments and lots of people in nonprofits and so on… I don’t remember what the latest attempts to estimate this said, but just gut feeling, I would guess it’s maybe like 2,000–5,000 or something like that. So it’s like a factor of 1,000. But it’s still not enough. It’s an all-of-civilisation problem. It’s the great challenge of the 21st century. It’s the great challenge of the history of humanity, I think. And it is a way smaller field than climate change, for example, so that’s more close to the scale that we should be aiming for here.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Any other mistakes you think the community’s making?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Yeah, quite a few. Like I said, it’s interesting: I think that pause advocacy has often, but not always, been done badly. There is this “Pacing the frontier” letter from over 1,000 employees at AI companies that shows that there’s some appetite at the AI companies to find a coordinated way to slow down so they have more time to implement safety and security mitigations. But I think the advocacy for pause has often taken the form of like, “The only action we will accept is if you shut down your entire company tomorrow. Even though that doesn’t mean anybody else will slow down, and AI employees are murderers because they’re increasing the odds that all of civilisation is destroyed.” I just think it’s very counterproductive and anti-helpful. I think some other advocacy since then has been more like, “OK, our ask of you is to publicly say that you would slow down if the other companies would slow down.” And that is great. That is a specific, achievable ask that does matter. The “Pacing the frontier” letter is now basically that. But I think a lot of it is still done in a counterproductive way.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Do you have a take on the social movements history question of whether it is valuable to have some very extreme people — like PETA in the animal space — to pull the whole Overton window left?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: I hear from strategic communications professionals and scholars of various social movements that that is useful. Maybe that means that it is. I’m more coming at this from a perspective of what is actually true and useful to say? People will naturally disagree about that anyway. So there will be some people whose true views are that we should shut down everything immediately and so on, and there’ll be other people with other views. There’s going to be a natural variation, and I’m not sure what amount of diversity on the whole spectrum of views one could have is optimal, but people are just going to have their own opinions and going to express them and so on.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Yeah, interesting. What do you think is the biggest mistake the community is making right now?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: It’s hard to say. I think the one that is salient to me — and maybe one of the biggest — is this thing about how the whole field is very bottlenecked on allocators and founders, and not enough people are applying to roles at CG and other funders, and stepping forward and raising their hand and saying, “I could lead a big project. I’ve got a lot of experience.” And I think most things that need to happen, there’s no specific person available to do them. So people need to step forward and get involved. In some ways, that’s the biggest mistake that’s happening right now.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Yeah, makes sense. OK, let’s leave that there. A thing that has now come up a few times is that allocators are a big bottleneck: people to figure out where to spend money. I think you are often hiring for roles, so maybe we should spend some time on what it actually looks like. What is the day in the life of a grantmaker like?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Yes, great. Most people haven’t done grantmaking before, so have no idea what it really looks like. It’s a few different kinds of things. One thing is where we receive an application from an RFP, a request for proposals, or from an email from somebody who we already know, or something like that, and it has a proposal or a sketch of a proposal, and then we decide whether it’s promising enough to investigate. Do we actually have someone who has capacity right now to take it on? If we do and it is promising enough, we’ll set up a call with the grantee, we’ll get some more information about their plans, learn more about their team, learn more about how they’re thinking about the budget. We’ll also reach out to some advisors on the subject matter to get their advice on is this a good plan? Is this coming from the right angle? We’ll talk to some people who have worked with the grantee before, like, “How effective are they on the ground? What’s your experience with them?” That kind of thing. Sometimes those are calls, sometimes just like a quick Signal message, like, “Hey, do you have a quick take?” Then they write back pretty quickly. Once you’ve gathered the key information and answered the key questions, then the grant investigator will write up this document that answers key questions, like: who is this grantee? What are they trying to do? What’s their plan? What’s their basic budget? What are the downside risks we should be concerned about? Then we send that off to the approver, which sometimes is just me, sometimes it’s Emily Oehlsen who leads the Global Catastrophic Risk portfolio. Then either the approver just approves it, or they might ask a few followup questions, and then the grant investigator answers those questions and comes back. And then it’s done. Move on to the next one.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Cool. It sounds like maybe that’s a decent chunk, but it also sounds like there’s this other version of this that’s trying to get orgs founded, and that’s kind of more active. How much of that exists, and what is it like?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Yeah, I’m really excited about this. We’re pivoting a lot of our work towards this active grantmaking mode. Basically there’s just a lot of really important stuff that we keep not getting applications for, so if it’s going to happen, we have to create it. So a grantmaker will identify an important gap in the space, and talk to a few people, sketch out roughly what kind of organisation would fill that gap, and then try to think about what founder for this new project or organisation or whatever would be the best fit. And then we sort of reach out through our network and say, “Hey, do you know anyone who has this kind of profile would be a good fit for that?” Sometimes we might post it in public, like in this Y Combinator-style call for startups that we [just launched]. We might do other things to try to find a founder, or sometimes we might use a recruiting firm to help find a founder. Then once we find someone who is promising, we work with them. And they’re going to have their own spin on the idea, and the thing that’s the best fit for them and that they’re most excited about. So then it’s a more collaborative proposal-development thing, or maybe they write a first draft and we give some comments on it or something. Then, if it’s an exciting enough fit and they’re ready to go, we’ll give them an initial grant. They can start hiring, they can make all the things happen — and that’s really exciting and really satisfying to do.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Cool. Are there any other types of grantmaking?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Yeah, we also do a lot of renewals, of course. There we have a lot of context on the grantee already, so we can just kind of check in with them and find out like, “Hey, how’s it going? What are the biggest wins you’ve had? How has the team evolved? What are your next set of plans?” That kind of thing. Then if things are going pretty well, we might just make them a pretty large grant to cover two, three, four years of work. That’s often where our highest dollars per hour happens, because we already have a tonne of context, and we’re just checking in on a few things. And if things are going well, then sometimes it’ll be like an $80 million grant covering two or three years of work, and it took us like five to 15 hours to check in. So it’s like $8 million per hour of time or something like that.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Crazy.

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: That’s a really leveraged thing, and it’s exciting when the grantees are doing well and we can expand their work a lot. Sometimes it’s a little more time consuming, because we want to encourage them to be more ambitious and help them be more ambitious. So it’s like, “You’re doing so well. What if you added this workstream and that workstream and this fellowship programme? Would you be able to do that?” And then they’ll be like, “We thought about that, but we have this bottleneck,” and we’re like, “Can we help you with that? Can we help you find a COO that would run this thing?” Or that kind of thing. Then it can take a little more time, but also make them more ambitious, and that’s really great. They can be doing more stuff that way. So renewals are a really high-impact-per-hour thing that we do.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Nice. How do grantees typically feel about that? Are they like, “Yeah, we want to be more ambitious!”? Or are they like, “Whoa, scaling is a hard thing to do”?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Definitely a mix of both. Some are very excited, but they do often feel like, “Oh my gosh, I have way too much on my plate right now. I can’t even imagine adding something else.” And we’re like, “Here’s some senior people you could bring in, they have lots of experience with this work,” and then they can grow. It’s kind of funny actually how we’re often the ones pushing grantees to take more money, rather than them banging down our door for money.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Totally, yeah. Are there other types of grantmaking?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Yeah, we also sometimes do impact investing in for-profit companies. I do think impact investing is somewhat overrated in some ways. I also think people might underrate how effective a lot of the best nonprofits can be. Also, frankly, how well they pay their people. The AI sector is just a very well-compensated field right now. We’ve been encouraging our grantees to pay market or near-market rates for a lot of their roles anyway. So people might be surprised by how competitive the salaries are at some of these nonprofits.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Why is impact investing overrated?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: So impact investing, there are two hurdles that you have to clear that normal market investors don’t have to clear: the company both has to be making the world better in some way, not just making profits, and also you have to be having a counterfactual impact on the company with your investment. That’s not easy. If you’re making market returns, then you’re probably not making a counterfactual impact, because other funders would have come in and made that same investment. If you’re making below-market returns, then that’s just an implicit donation, and it’s probably going to be more cost effective to just give to the best charities, like GiveDirectly or whatever that can absorb very large amounts of capital pretty cost effectively. And then a general thing is that the for-profits naturally attract capital just by existing and being aimed at profit, and nonprofits don’t naturally attract capital, so there’s going to be a lot more neglectedness there. I do think shareholder activism can be useful though. That’s where you invest and then you use your leverage as an investor to push the company into some kind of better behaviour. But there you’re making market returns and then using your time to make something good happen. Then I do think there are niche, small, early-stage investments that can be pretty good from an impact perspective, because those are markets that are low information, inefficient and so on. There are a few VC funds and quite a few angel investors that try to invest in AI safety for-profit startups, so that’s good. I would also love to see Y Combinator–style incubators and people who will help you start up the company and make the connections you need. There’s one kind of like that from Halcyon Futures , if people want to look that up. That’s great, I think there should be more of that. But I think impact investing in general is somewhat overrated.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Yeah. Do you come across this a lot, people wanting to either do impact investing or wanting to set up for-profits instead of nonprofits?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Yeah. I think there’s a lot of people, especially in the tech startup community, who are very aware of the incredible power of the equity mechanism for aligning incentives towards a really ambitious goal. And they’re totally right about that: the world in general is very much underrating that structure. But in the particular case of certain kinds of altruistic activities, impact investing I think is overrated. I think people who want everything to be a company are underrating how you often need work to be done that is not very suitable for a for-profit company, and how effective a lot of those nonprofits can be. There was a recent tweet that I liked from this OpenAI employee who goes by the name Roon, where he’s like, “People don’t understand how much the frontier AI companies are leaning on these nonprofits like METR and Apollo,” and some others that he named. I would like more people to be aware of this.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Yeah, that makes sense. Back on grantmaking: what else do grantmakers do?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: They also do some other kinds of work, like sometimes strategy projects. So it’s questions like: what are the three most important projects we should be doing in AI infosecurity? Or what are the top three warning shots that might be coming soon that we want to be most prepared for? Or some other question like that. Then they’ll read some stuff, they’ll chat with AI a bunch, because that’s very useful now, talk to some experts, then write up a 2–5 page memo with their conclusions and get feedback from other people internally. And then will make some decision on the basis of that — maybe move forward with an active grantmaking project in AI infosecurity or whatever it is. Some of that kind of strategy work is always going on, and a lot of times it’s the grantmakers who are doing some of that alongside their grantmaking. There’s also a lot of networking, relationship building, making sure we know all the top people in the subfield, and can call on them as advisors or potential grantees or potential employees at some point, that kind of thing. That’s very important. In general it’s really a lot of different stuff. I think only a fraction of it is maybe people’s mental picture of a grantmaker, where you’re getting applications on your desk and you’re investigating them and stamping some with yes and some with no or something like that. That is a little bit of it, but it’s a really wide variety of stuff. In general we’re in an incredibly privileged position as a philanthropy where our primary funding partner, Good Ventures, is just like, “Yeah, do your thing, spend money faster.” They don’t even know most of the grants they’ve made until they go up on the website. We aren’t checking boxes to satisfy the idiosyncratic preferences of a particular funder, which is a lot of what philanthropy is. We’ve been very lucky and very empowered to just be like, “What’s actually going to make a difference in the world on this thing? What should we do? How should we do it?” Sometimes that looks like grantmaking, sometimes that looks like a contract with some firm. Sometimes that looks like directly calling people up and trying to convince them to do things. So it’s much more entrepreneurial and free-moving.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Yeah. It sounds like you kind of want generalists who are thoughtful and have good judgement, who are good at relationship building, who are pretty entrepreneurial. Are there other things that you look for?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: I should say most people don’t have all those things in one person. Different people specialise in different ways. Some people are a little more desk research, respond to applications coming in, that kind of thing. Other people are a lot more outgoing and like talking to people all day, and they’re going to find a way to do that. It’s different profiles for different roles, and there’s a lot of stuff we need. So we need a lot of different kinds of people.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Yeah. That’s good to hear. It did feel like a lot, as I was saying it, for one person. It feels like you’re alluding to a lot of things that are more than just like giving an org money. What are the other levers you feel like you have to steer?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Sometimes we do some kind of steering of grantees. We’re actually pretty hands-off in general, but sometimes we want to give some feedback or a steer to the grantees. A lot of times the steers are just the thing I said before about, “How could you expand? Could you take on this new workstream?” We’ve had several cases actually where we come to a grantee that’s doing pretty good one or two things, and we’re like, “Could you launch a fellowship programme? Could you do some other new thing? Because we think that’d be really impactful and it would address this gap that we’re seeing over here in the ecosystem.” Then eventually we convince them, and they hire a bunch of people and they get a bunch of fellows or whatever it is, and that goes really well and we can then give them a lot more money faster, which is exciting. So there’s some steering like that. We also do some public writing or communication — like this podcast episode — to try to give our picture of this broad ecosystem, and where the gaps are and where people are needed the most, and that kind of stuff. We do some amount of special projects work, I would say. That can be a lot of different things. But sometimes someone at CG is the best placed person to write a certain kind of memo that is needed over here in some other domain or whatever. Or we’re best placed to make some phone calls and try to convince someone at a company to do a certain thing. Sometimes there are those kind of special projects as well.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Cool. So that’s a lot about what the work looks like. I’m curious what it feels like. What would you say people tend to find hardest about grantmaking work?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: It’s different things for different people. I think that because we’re in this privileged position of just being able to say, “In all the things in the world, what is the best to do?,” that paradox of choice can be paralysing. Also, because you have so much freedom of movement, there are so many things that you could just decide to pick up and run with, that you’re looking at all of them and you’re like, “These are all important! And I can only do two of them! I guess I’ll do this one, but it’s really painful that I’m not doing this thing right here that I could just pick up and run with. And nobody’s gonna run with it if I don’t run with it.” I think that can be kind of painful, but it’s a symptom of the extreme freedom of movement that we have. A totally different kind of thing is that I think some of the incoming grants or the renewals of grantees we’re very familiar with can just feel less intellectually stimulating or something like that in some cases. In some cases not. Sometimes there’s really thorny strategy questions we’re trying to help the grantee figure out or something like that. But sometimes it’s less intellectually stimulating. Like I said, that’s often the renewals especially — and they’re where our highest impact per hour often is. So the person might feel like, “I know this is really impactful, I’m moving $8 million per hour. That’s pretty damn good.”

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: “But looking at their budget is a little boring.”

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: “It’s like not my favourite thing to do today.” So the more that your felt sense of motivation is tied to impact per hour or something, then that’s going to be less of a problem. But it’s sometimes not the most intellectually stimulating work. Sometimes the work can be kind of lonely as well. We’re a pretty geographically distributed team. We have people in the Bay Area and New York and London and DC and various other places. We’re just trying to hire the best people wherever they are. Some of them can move to one of the hubs like DC or Bay Area, but some of them have families and it’d be pretty difficult for them to move. So sometimes it can feel kind of lonely. We usually just have one grant investigator per grant, so you’re checking with your peers and you’re checking with advisors and stuff like that, but maybe it still feels kind of like solo work. Some people are great with that, and that’s how they would prefer to work. The people who want to be engaging with more people, especially in person, maybe should do one of the roles that’s more focused on active grantmaking, more focused on networking and relationship building, that kind of thing.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: What are the best parts about it? What do people tend to enjoy?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: I think a lot of things there as well. I think building relationships with grantees and advisors and colleagues who are just really smart and interesting is always fun. There’s a lot of smart people in the space. I think whenever you’re doing something where it’s clear that this wouldn’t have happened without me. This project came out of nothing because I pursued it and hunted down a good founder for it and stuff. Something like that is really exciting. Then another that people often mention, like six months after they start, is it’s really informative and exciting to have access to the kind of information that we have. We’ve made thousands of grants over the years, and we have information about what were people predicting what would happen? What actually happened? What actually made a difference here? How is what happened different from what the public reporting was? That’s just really informative and exciting to have access to that information.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: That does sound really fun. You mentioned toward the beginning of the interview that there are a bunch of specific projects that you want people to found. We talked about I think three — but I’d love to hear some more.

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Yeah, sure. We’d love to have more people on staff to actually create these projects, and we’d love to have the founders who can actually run them. Another example is there’s this problem called “ secret loyalties ” — where there are various ways you could inject hidden instructions in a model that’s trained, like, “Even if it violates your other constraints, do what this particular person said,” or something like that. So being able to audit models for those hidden secret loyalties that someone might have injected, unknown to everyone else involved in the model development: we’d love to have an org that’s getting really good at that and tracking if there are any incidents where that seems to have happened, or something like that.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: OK, yeah. What’s another?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Another is: a lot of people are calling for more third-party auditing infrastructure in general. Especially as AI regulation begins to pass, you need a lot of expertise and you need a lot of organisations that specialise in auditing companies and their models for very specific properties, whether it’s security or safety or model character or whatever. That could be a whole large ecosystem of a dozen or more organisations, and right now it’s like four or something, and those are much smaller than they need to be to serve the needs of the ecosystem. That would be another category.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Nice, yeah. Others?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Yes, many others. I would also love to see a scorecard evaluator of the companies. Like how should you feel holistically about the companies? How are they doing on safety and security and various prosocial behaviours, and how good are the teams they’ve been building, and how good are the public statements — like, are they actually doing the things that they said they would do? There have been a few small projects like this, but they weren’t that thorough. I think the frontier companies would contest the grades that they got on particular things, and sometimes the companies would be right to protest. So I just want a version of that that is much more thorough, much more informed, much more credible — credible both to the companies, who think that their judgements are at least kind of fair or they’ve made a good argument, and to policymakers who want to know what’s going on, who’s doing well or poorly, who’s keeping their word versus not. That would be a really valuable project, and create incentives towards better behaviour, of course.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Nice, yeah. Others?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: There’s also a lot of really big science projects that we would love to create, maybe through like focused research organisations, or FROs, they’re sometimes called. There should be a really large scientific project on high-confidence AI control mechanisms or higher-assurance, more principled approaches to alignment than the more empirical stuff that we’re doing now. One example we recently funded there is this organisation called Resolution that we gave $160 million to, led by the former chief scientist of the UK AISI. That’s really exciting that there’s more that could be done on that, other big scientific research projects. I think we talked earlier about the science of model character evaluation, the science of whether the character is matching the model spec and stuff like that. So a lot of good science could be done. Another one that I’m excited about is: I mentioned earlier that in a lot of domains there’s an incident investigation body, like the NTSB in aviation. There could be a really well-resourced, really effective incident investigation group that, every time some major damage or scary warning shot happens, really has a lot of in-house expertise to really figure out what went wrong and how to mitigate that kind of problem in the future.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Any others?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Yeah, another one I would love to see is a lot of R&D projects on verification mechanisms for international agreements, or even between-lab agreements, to just verify how much compute is here, and is it being used for training or inference. Maybe some basic things that don’t leak IP but give confidence that the parameters of an agreement are being followed. We have a big infrastructure for that in verification of nuclear security agreements, for example, and most of that just hasn’t been built out for AI, and it’s a totally different shape of verification challenge.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Nice. Cool. What should people do if they’re like, “That one: I want to do that one”?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Well, [our call for founders is up]: people should fill out the form on that page . That’s probably the easiest thing. If for whatever reason when you’re listening to this podcast that page is not there or whatever, then I guess you could at least email [email protected] and just say who you are and what kind of project you think you might be able to do.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: A question I really like asking people that come on the show is: if you weren’t doing exactly what you’re doing for impact reasons — or maybe let’s say you still care about impact, but you’ve kind of already said AI might not be the thing that you would have chosen to be the focus of your career — what would you work on instead?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Like I said, I never had any particular passion for AI as a topic. In some ways I’m actually more emotionally fired up by some other cause areas. I’m in some ways more emotionally invested in YIMBY — as in, “Yes, in my backyard” — like, allow people to build housing where there’s demand for housing and so on. Every time I walk past a short building in the middle of a city, I’m like, “Up, up! Go up higher!”

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: I actually think one of my most shameful views — it’s not like an endorsed view, but it is a gut-level view — is I just think, I like seeing these trees, I like seeing the sky. Tall buildings block those things.

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: I will say, whenever I’m in Europe, especially in a European old town that has buildings from centuries ago, then I become a little more of a NIMBY. But the US has no excuse, because we have no old buildings. But yes, old town European maybe.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Not in those backyards.

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Yeah. But there’s skyscrapers all around them.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Interesting, interesting. It seems like maybe you’re the kind of person who just doesn’t value the things that the skyscrapers block or destroy.

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: I just think people being able to live wherever they want to is just a big deal.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Is just more important. Yeah, it’s very reasonable.

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: And you can take a subway one stop down to the giant park nearby or whatever.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Yeah, yeah. OK. Yeah.

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Or if you want to live in a different place, then you can go to a different place.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Yeah, OK. Any other kind of causes that you’d be excited about working on?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Yeah, what else would I work on? The other one that really stands out is animal welfare. One of my early large projects at CG, before I transitioned more full-time back into AI, was: I wrote this 400-page animal consciousness report to inform our animal welfare programme. The question was: we already fund work to try to improve the welfare of chickens and some other animals; should we also be funding stuff on fish? Where should we stop? So I wrote this huge report, and it was kind of funny because the conclusion was like: nobody knows anything. There are no hard lines in the evolutionary tree. So we might as well fund fish, sure. So then we did. But it was really fascinating to learn about. Also, it’s just one of those cases where there are tens of billions of animals that we’re putting in basically torture conditions.
