That’s just totally crazy. We could just not do that. I have huge respect for vegans and vegetarians. I’m very fired up about this cause emotionally. There should be a lot more work on it. I’m really proud of and excited by the work that the CG Farm Animal Welfare programme does.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Yeah. On the animal stuff, I care about this very, very much, but I feel like sometimes I lose touch with how meaningful it is to still improve things now. One, AI is this massive deal. And two, it’s coming relatively soon. If we make things go well, it can help a lot with all these other problems. Then I pause for a second and I’m like: there are still billions of animals being tortured right now . It is still really terrible. I feel like it’s good, even if it’s not the thing I want to work on, to be like, that torture right now matters, even though AI also matters. I guess I’m curious, I think at times I have found it kind of hard to be like, “I’m really intrinsically and emotionally motivated to work on and learn about and use the podcast to cover certain topics. But I should probably focus on these things that are more important given limited resources.” How have you found it?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Yeah, I’ve been working most of the time, not the whole time, on AI — since I guess 2010. That was entirely just because I thought it was the most important thing, not because I have any intrinsic interest in AI. It’s very satisfying to work on something that you think is very important, and it’s exciting to work in a field that is moving as fast and becoming a bigger deal every year and that kind of stuff. That’s all very gratifying, but it is also a very scary field to work in . We are just thinking about possible ends of the world and how to avoid the end of the world and stuff. That’s just somewhat emotionally draining. I do personally get a lot of value out of separating my thinking about work stuff and thinking about personal life and hobbies and hanging out with my wife and stuff like that. That’s great. I spend a lot of time touching grass or touching moss if possible, and going on hikes and just staring at beautiful trees. So that’s very helpful.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: So you have like a bucket for personal fulfilment? On the “it’s hard to work on this” thing, sometimes I’m like, I don’t feel it enough in my bones. Then other times I feel it so much in my bones, I can’t live like this.

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Right, right.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: How often do you spend in these spaces? And how do you find it?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: I bet different strategies are better for different people. I’m curious what your strategy is. But I think for my temperament and emotional state, I can almost get to a place where I’ve just emotionally accepted that we’re in this very extreme and dangerous situation, and I’m just kind of treating it more as like a chess puzzle that I’m trying to solve, and I’m kind of screening off how important is this chess puzzle? Then it’s more when I get back to high-level prioritisation and strategy, where I’m trying to engage with exactly how important is this chunk of the work versus this chunk of the work, because of how it connects to different possible ends of the world and stuff like that… I don’t know if that would work for someone else, but you can be in chess-puzzle mode for a while and not having it necessarily connect to “if you make the wrong move here, everyone dies.”

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Right, right. Yeah. Do you kind of endorse not spending that much time in the “everyone dies” part?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Probably for most people that’s wise. Some people could have a psychology that can tolerate that. I’m probably not one of them.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Yeah. Cool. I don’t know actually what the proportions are, but every time I try to be like, “OK, I’m gonna feel it a bit more, and maybe that will have some positive effects on motivation, and maybe it’ll help me track which things are most important a bit more,” then I try a little bit, and I’m like, “Whoa! That’s not something I can handle.”

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Time to go touch some grass.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Yeah, exactly. So compartmentalising is a thing we both do, I think.

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: OK, we have time for one more question. Let’s say we win, and we’ve reached superabundance, and we can do what we want and have all the things. What are you going to be spending your time and consciousness on?

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Yeah, that would be nice. Let’s try to do it. I have, like most people, a lot of hobbies. Or I have a lot of hobbies that I wish I had time for. One I’ll mention is that I’m really into contemporary classical music — so like new symphonies, concertos, string quartets that they wrote in the last 50 years or whatever. Most of the pieces that have been composed have never been recorded, so you can’t listen to them unless you travel specifically to Vienna on October 3 or something. So, I don’t know, I guess I would have robot orchestras performing and recording all the pieces. Then I would love to compose music myself, and learn how to compose music first. I listen to all this stuff and it sparks all these ideas about, “I would elaborate this musical idea” or something. Obviously I don’t have the time or skill right now to compose those pieces, but I would love to do that. That would be really fun. But to get there, people have to pivot into AI safety.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Quit your jobs.

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Yeah, quit your jobs. Get a career transition grant , apply to CG , apply to other funders, apply to be a founder of these projects that need to exist. We got to do that really fast right now.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Yeah, yeah. It feels like that’s the homework, and then we get to have the summer holiday.

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: Yeah. I would love the glorious solarpunk future where I get to compose contemporary classical music, and you can do whatever you want to do, but we have to solve the problem first.

turns.speaker: Luisa Rodriguez
turns.text: Yep. My guest today has been Luke Muehlhauser. Thanks so much for coming on.

turns.speaker: Luke Muehlhauser
turns.text: It’s been a pleasure.
